title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals used generative AI to create deepfakes and clone voices of real people, then deployed these fabrications on social media and through phone calls to impersonate immigration attorneys and trusted contacts. The scams targeted immigrants and others vulnerable to urgent requests, with reported losses in the millions of dollars across Georgia and South Florida. This is impersonation enabled by synthetic media, deployed without any verification step to check whether the voice or image matched a real person before accepting money.

The failure happened at the point where victims had no reliable way to verify they were communicating with the person they thought they were. The technology made impersonation easier and more convincing than traditional methods. Detection would have required either independent verification by the victim, like calling the attorney through a number they sourced themselves, or friction in the payment process that forced verification before funds moved.

It is not established how the scammers obtained the source material for the voice cloning or whether any particular AI system was modified to enable this use, only that generative AI tools were used in the commission of fraud.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit fraud by creating deepfakes and cloning voices to impersonate trusted individuals. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice was cloned to target immigrants and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. The FBI received over 1 million internet crime complaints totaling more than $20 billion in reported losses overall. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints with $10.4 million in losses, though these figures likely undercount the actual problem.

Scammers use generative AI to clone voices from social media videos, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal relationships to make their schemes more convincing. The technology has particularly enhanced romance scams, distress scams, and the grandparent scam. Financial institutions warn that verification is becoming increasingly difficult. Authorities recommend establishing code words with family members, verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, and never sending money based solely on phone calls. The FBI advises reporting suspected scams to local law enforcement and freezing credit if identity theft is suspected.
